desc:
Numbers arrive one at a time in the order of nums. After each arrival, the median of everything received so far is defined: the middle value of the sorted numbers for an odd count, or the average of the two middle values for an even count.

Count how many arrivals made the median strictly larger than it was right after the previous arrival. The first arrival has no predecessor and never counts.

nums = [5, 2, 8, 1, 9, 9]
medians after each arrival: 5, 3.5, 5, 3.5, 5, 6.5
rises: 3.5 -> 5, 3.5 -> 5, 5 -> 6.5   so the answer is 3
hints: Sorting every prefix is too slow for large inputs; you only need the middle of the sorted prefix.
To avoid fractions, compare twice the median: the middle value doubled for an odd count, the sum of the two middle values for an even count.
Keep the lower half in a max-heap and the upper half in a min-heap with sizes differing by at most one, then read the median from the two roots after each insertion.
editorial: Maintain two heaps: lo, a max-heap with the smaller half (it gets the extra element when the count is odd), and hi, a min-heap with the larger half. A new number goes into lo if it is at most the root of lo, otherwise into hi; then one root is moved across if the sizes drift apart by more than allowed.

After each insertion the doubled median is 2 * lo.root for an odd count and lo.root + hi.root for an even count. Comparing doubled medians with the previous one counts the rises with exact integer arithmetic.
Each insertion costs O(log n), so the total is O(n log n) time and O(n) space. Doubled values reach at most 2 * 10<sup>9</sup>, which still fits a signed 32-bit integer.
